en: *Jingxun for the Gate of the Black Robe*, Scroll One:
The *Caishi* (Warning) of Chan Master Dayuan of Mount Gui.
Now, being bound by karma to receive a body, one cannot avoid the burdens of form. Having received the physical frame bequeathed by one's parents, one relies upon the various [elements].
They are formed together through conditions;
though sustained by the four great elements,
they are constantly in mutual opposition.
Impermanence, old age, and sickness do not wait for an appointment with anyone;
one may exist in the morning and perish by evening, changing worlds in a single kṣaṇa.
It is like spring frost or morning dew, which vanish in an instant.
The trees on the bank and the vines by the well— how could they endure for long?
Moments pass with such rapidity that in a single kṣaṇa, the shifting of one breath is already the next life.
Why do you remain so complacent and let time pass in vain?
Your parents no longer provide you with delicacies,
and your six kin have surely abandoned you.
Unable to bring peace to his state or govern his nation,
he suddenly abandoned his family estate and his lineage.
He distantly left his native village, shaved his hair, and received the precepts from a master.
Inwardly, he diligently applied himself to the practice of mindfulness;
outwardly, he propagated the virtue of non-contention.
Having completely detached from the mundane world, he aspired for liberation.
How is it that as soon as one has ascended to the level of the precepts,
one immediately declares, "I am a bhikṣu," and partakes of whatever food and requisites the donor provides?
They remained constantly without reflection or contemplation;
regarding their place of origin, they claimed it was simply "the nature of things" (*dharmatā*).
Having finished eating together, they gathered their heads together in noisy chatter.
They speak only of miscellaneous worldly matters;
thus, they seek pleasure for the duration of their lives,
unaware that such pleasure is the cause of suffering.
Throughout past kalpas, I have pursued the dust of the world without ever reflecting upon it;
time has been wasted and years have slipped away.
My enjoyments have been abundant and my gains and benefits have been rich and thick.
Passing through years and decades without doubting their abandonment,
they have accumulated vast stores while maintaining this illusory physical form.
The Teacher has issued a command to admonish and exhort the bhikṣus.
In advancing on the Path and adorning the person, these three are always insufficient;
yet most people indulge in their flavors without ceasing,
so that as days pass and months come, they suddenly find themselves with white hair.
Those of later learning who have not yet heard the essential purport must extensively consult those who know it beforehand;
for while they might think that leaving the household life is valued merely for the sake of seeking food and clothing, the Buddha first established the Vinaya.
He initiated the rules and decorum for those beginning their studies,
making them as pure as ice and snow;
through the observance of prohibitions and the performance of duties, he restrained and disciplined those at the stage of the initial mind.
The subtle precepts have rectified various vulgar abuses;
yet I have never had the honor of participating in a *vinaya* assembly,
so how could I possibly discern the definitive meaning of the Supreme Vehicle?
It is a pity that one’s entire life has passed in vain;
regret is difficult to undo once it has arisen.
One has never applied oneself to the teachings and principles of the Dharma.
The profound Way is realized without cause;
yet as one grows old and their years increase,
they remain empty-minded and arrogant, refusing to draw near to virtuous friends.
Knowing only arrogance and being unacquainted with the laws and regulations,
they lack all sense of restraint;
at times they speak loudly and in high voices, uttering words without moderation.
They show no respect for elders, those of middle rank, or juniors;
they gather like a Brahmin assembly without distinction.
They make noise with their bowls and alms-basins, and they rise before the meal is finished.
Their conduct is erratic and contrary to principle, entirely lacking the essence of a monk;
they are agitated whether rising or sitting, disturbing the thoughts of others,
and they do not maintain even the slightest rules or minor points of decorum.
How can these be gathered and restrained?
Future generations and those newly entering the study [of the Way] will have no basis upon which to model themselves;
they will merely become aware of one another's failings.
He then said, "I am a mountain monk.
I have not heard the Buddha's teachings;
my practice has consistently been coarse in nature."
Such a view is merely for those at the beginning of their practice.
Through indolence, gluttony, and complacency, time slips away;
thus, one gradually becomes estranged from the human world without even realizing it.
A decrepit old man, stumbling at every step and facing a wall whenever he encounters anything;
when later students come to inquire, he has no words with which to guide them,
and even if he does speak, his discourse does not touch upon the subtle or the formal.
Or perhaps, upon being addressed with slighting words, they immediately rebuke their juniors;
out of impoliteness, anger arises in their hearts, and they speak harshly.
They speak of others who have suddenly fallen ill and lie bedridden.
Entangled and oppressed by manifold sufferings,
they contemplate day and night with hearts filled with agitation;
the path ahead is vast and desolate, and they know not where it leads.
From this point on, I have finally come to know how to repent my transgressions.
To dig a well only when one is thirsty—what use is that? Why do I harbor such self-reproach?
Had I not cultivated myself early on, many faults and failings would abound in my later years.
As they approach their departure, they squander their resources in a state of terror and frantic alarm;
as the grain is pierced through and sparrows fly away,
the consciousness-mind follows its karma like a person burdened by debt.
The strong lead the way, while the mind’s tendencies are manifold;
it falls heavily toward whatever is most weighty.
The demon of impermanence that kills does not pause for a single thought-moment.
Life cannot be extended and time cannot be waited for;
even those in the three realms of existence among humans and devas cannot escape this.
Thus, receiving such a body is not a matter of calculating kalpas.
Filled with sorrow, lamentation, and wonder, my grief cuts to the core of my heart.
How can we remain silent? We must instead exhort one another.
What I regret is that we have been born in this age of semblance-dharma, far removed from the time of the Sage.
Those whose understanding of the Buddha-dharma is superficial often fall into indolence;
I shall briefly set forth my humble views to enlighten those who come after.
If you do not cast off your self-conceit, [you will fail].
It is truly difficult to evade this cycle of rebirth.
Now, those who have left the household life set out with their feet toward the transcendental realm; their minds and forms differ from the mundane world.
They perpetuate the lineage of the Sages and strike terror into the armies of Māra.
One employs this to repay the four debts of gratitude and to deliver beings from the three realms of existence.
If one does not act thus,
one will improperly join the ranks of the Sangha while one's speech and conduct remain negligent and coarse.
In vain have I partaken of the offerings of the faithful.
The places where I once traveled have not moved a single inch;
in this daze, for a lifetime, what can I rely upon?
How much more so for those with the majestic appearance of a monk, whose countenances are worthy of admiration;
all have planted roots of goodness in past lives to evoke such extraordinary retribution,
and thus they ought to remain composed with hands folded in reverence.
If one does not value even a moment of time, one's undertakings will not be diligent;
without the causes for merit and fruition, how could they ever be accomplished?
How could one possibly let a lifetime pass in vain?
Furthermore, his future karma was free from obstruction;
he took leave of his kin and resolved to don the black robes.
His intention was to transcend all equally, and what did he contemplate throughout the day and night?
How could one possibly delay until time has passed?
One’s heart should aspire to serve as a pillar for the Buddha-dharma,
acting as a model and mirror for future generations.
I have always felt that I am unable to correspond even slightly with such standards;
my speech must involve the classical canons,
and my discourse must rely upon antiquity.
His physical bearing was upright and distinctive, and his spirit was lofty, tranquil, and remote.
In his conduct, he required the assistance of virtuous friends,
for they frequently purified his ears and eyes.
One must carefully choose one's companions when dwelling;
from time to time, one should hear what has not yet been heard.
Thus it is said:
Those who give birth to me are my parents;
those who bring me to fulfillment are my friends.
To draw near to the virtuous is like walking amidst mist and dew.
Although they do not soak their robes, they are occasionally moistened by it;
associating with the wicked, they cultivate evil views and commit evil deeds from dawn until dusk.
Immediately upon death, one receives retribution and sinks into the depths of suffering;
once lost, this human body will not be regained for ten thousand kalpas.
These are words of loyalty that are contrary to the ear.
Is this not something that should be engraved upon one's heart?
It enables one to cleanse the mind,
nurture virtue, obscure one's traces, conceal one's fame, and preserve one's inner purity.
If you wish to engage in Zen meditation and study the Way, you must bring this clamor of the spirit to a complete halt.
This is the gateway of sudden transcendence and skillful means;
the mind accords with the profound ford, investigating the subtle and the exquisite,
discerning the deep and the abstruse, and awakening to the true source.
Seek out those of vast learning and prior realization, and draw near to virtuous friends;
for the subtle essence of this school is difficult to attain,
one must apply oneself with meticulous care.
One may therein suddenly awaken to the True Cause;
this is precisely the gradual stage for transcending the mundane world.
This constitutes the shattering of the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms.
Know that all internal and external phenomena are entirely unreal;
arising from the transformations of the mind, they are all merely provisional names.
Do not employ the mind to settle or dwell upon them.
But if the mind does not cling to objects, how could objects obstruct the person?
Let the Dharma-nature flow freely as it will; neither sever it nor continue it.
Hearing sounds and seeing forms is but the ordinary;
whether at this shore or that shore, one’s practical application should be without deficiency.
To act and abide in such a manner is truly not to wear the Dharma robes in vain.
Furthermore, one thereby repays the four debts of gratitude and delivers beings from the three realms of existence.
If one can remain steadfast in this practice throughout every lifetime without regression,
the stage of Buddhahood may certainly be expected.
A guest who comes and goes through the three realms,
appearing and disappearing for the sake of others—
this single practice is the most wondrous and profound.
Simply cultivate a resolute mind and you will certainly not be deceived.
If there are those of middling capacity who have not yet been able to transcend suddenly, [you must apply yourself].
Furthermore, apply your mind to the teachings;
study the palm-leaf manuscripts with diligence to thoroughly investigate their principles and meanings;
and transmit, chant, and propagate them to guide future generations.
To repay the Buddha’s kindness and virtue,
one must not let this time be wasted in vain;
it is essential that one sustain oneself by means of this.
Abiding in proper deportment is itself being a vessel of the Dharma within the Sangha.
Have you not seen how the climbing vine that leans upon a pine tree soars to a height of a thousand fathoms?
Only by relying on a superior cause can one bring about vast benefit.
Diligently cultivate the fasts and precepts; do not allow them to be violated or neglected.
Throughout every life and every rebirth, the extraordinary and wondrous causes and effects are not to be treated with indifference as one passes the days or idly spends the time.
What a pity that you waste your time,
seeking no spiritual advancement,
and merely squandering the offerings of the faithful from the ten directions.
Furthermore, one would fail the four debts of gratitude;
these accumulations grow ever deeper,
the dust of the mind easily becomes obstructed, and one encounters stagnation at every turn.
One is thus slighted and deceived by others.
As it was said of old:
"Since he is a man of stature, so am I."
One should not disparage oneself and become disheartened;
if one does not do so, one will merely remain within the gates of the monastic community for an entire life,
passing the time in vain without any benefit whatsoever.
I humbly hope that you will rouse a resolute will and open a magnanimous mind;
let your every action be modeled after those of the highest caliber.
Do not arbitrarily follow what is vulgar and base.
In this life, you must immediately resolve and discern;
do not rely on others, but quiet your mind and let go of all conditions.
Do not oppose the various sensory objects;
let the mind be empty and the environment be still.
This is simply because one has long been obstructed and stuck.
Study this text thoroughly and use it to admonish yourself at all times.
Exert firm mastery over yourself and do not yield to worldly sentiments;
for when one is pulled by the fruits of one's karma, it is truly difficult to escape.
When sounds are harmonious, echoes follow suit; when forms are straight, shadows are upright.
Cause and effect are thus clearly manifest—how could one not feel anxiety and dread?
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
Even if it be hundreds of thousands of eons,
the karma one has created does not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, [the fruit ripens].
The retribution returns to oneself to be experienced.
Thus, one should know that the punishments and fetters of the triple world kill people;
exert yourself in diligent cultivation and do not let the days pass in vain.
Only after deeply understanding the faults and perils did we urge one another to practice and uphold [the teachings].
We vow that for hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes, we shall always be dharma companions wherever we may be.
Thus, he composed this inscription:
The illusory body and dream-like dwelling are but objects within the void;
their prior limit is infinite, so how could their subsequent limit ever be reached?
Emerging here and perishing there, rising and sinking, one becomes utterly exhausted.
One cannot avoid the three wheels; when will there be rest?
Clinging to the world, the aggregates and conditions form a solid substance.
From birth until old age, one gains nothing at all.
Fundamental ignorance causes one to be deluded thereby;
time is precious, yet every moment is unpredictable.
This life passes in vain, while the next remains obstructed.
From delusion to further delusion, it is all due to the six thieves;
wandering through the six realms and crawling through the three worlds,
one should early seek out an enlightened teacher and draw near to those of high virtue.
Discriminate between body and mind to remove their thorns;
the world is inherently empty and illusory—how could the myriad conditions constrain you?
Investigate the principles of the Dharma, taking awakening as your standard.
Abandon both mind and objects; neither record nor recollect.
Let the six sense faculties be at ease, and remain silent and still in all movement and rest.
When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are simultaneously stilled.
The Chapter on Honoring the Sangha by Chan Master Mingjiao Song. Why must the Teaching necessarily honor the Sangha?
It is because those who are members of the Sangha take the Buddha as their nature.
They take the Tathāgata as their family,
the Dharma as their body,
and wisdom as their life.
Taking the joy of dhyāna as their sustenance,
they do not rely upon worldly people nor do they seek to establish a family lineage.
One does not cultivate the physical form;
one neither craves life nor fears death,
and is not steeped in the five flavors.
In guarding the body there is precept;
in collecting the mind there is concentration;
in discerning and clarifying there is wisdom.
Regarding his precepts, he purified the three delusions and remained untainted throughout his life;
regarding his concentration, he stilled his thoughts and maintained rectitude.
He was sagely and remained undisturbed throughout the entire day;
this speaks to his wisdom.
He honored virtue and discerned delusion with absolute necessity.
To cultivate by means of this is called the cause;
to accomplish by means of this is called the fruit.
Toward all beings, one possesses both loving-kindness and compassion.
There is a great vow and there is great benevolence. As for compassion,
it is the desire to bring peace to all things.
"Compassion" means constantly desiring to rescue all from suffering;
"vow" means...
I vow to see the True Dharma together with all under heaven.
As for "beneficence," it means bestowing the Right Dharma upon all living beings.
When one attains spiritual penetration,
even Heaven and Earth cannot obscure it;
when one practices with profound secrecy, [it becomes manifest].
Even spirits and deities could not fathom him.
In expounding the Dharma, his eloquence was unhindered;
in protecting the Dharma, he exerted himself without regard for his own person.
He can endure what others cannot endure and perform what others cannot perform.
As for his right livelihood, he eats food obtained by begging yet feels no shame.
In their fewness of desires, they wear ragged robes and carry patched bowls yet do not consider themselves poor.
In their lack of contention, they may be humiliated but cannot be slighted.
In their freedom from resentment, they can be associated with others but cannot be diminished.
He treated all things with reality and cultivated himself with supreme compassion;
thus, regarding the world, he was as follows.
He is able to be consistently harmonious and universally respectful.
Because his speech is free from falsehood, his integrity is ultimate.
Because his dharma is without self, his yielding is sincere.
Possessing an awe-inspiring presence that can warn and a dignified demeanor that can serve as a model,
celestial beings and humans alike look upon him with solemn reverence;
he is able to bestow blessings upon the world and guide the common people.
In his state of forgetting the physical form, he was cast among birds and beasts without feeling strange.
In his recitation and study, he braved cold and heat without ceasing.
Departing according to the Dharma, he wandered among humans throughout all the villages.
View names as echoes in a valley;
view profit as drifting dust;
view the colors of objects as the fleeting brilliance of sunlight.
He nurtures the poor and the sick and gathers with them like tiles and pebbles,
yet he does not consider himself base,
for he dwells according to the Way even in deep mountains and remote valleys.
They wear garments of grass and eat food from trees;
they are serene and self-sufficient,
and cannot be enticed by worldly gain.
One cannot be brought to submission by power.
To decline the titles of Son of Heaven or feudal lord is not considered haughtiness;
rather, one stands alone because one has achieved self-mastery through the Way.
Although they may have only their own forms and shadows for companions, they are not solitary;
though they dwell in groups, they are bound together by the Dharma;
and though they gather people from all quarters of the world, they do not become a chaotic mixture.
That which can be learned includes not only the Three Piṭakas and the Twelve Divisions of the Canon,
but even the books of the hundred schools and heterodox paths—
there is nothing he does not know.
Furthermore, there was no foreign dialect with which he was not proficient.
In his exposition of the Dharma, he possessed both literary elegance and structural coherence.
In practicing the Middle Way, he adhered to neither emptiness nor existence.
As for his abandonment of study, he was free from discursive thought, pure, and of singular, true suchness;
he no longer engaged in any further discrimination.
How eminent was he as a person! How truly a *saṃgha* he was!
His mind was vast;
his virtue was complete;
his Way was great.
Their being "worthy" is not what the world calls worthiness;
their being "sages" is not what the world calls sagehood.
They are the exceptionally superior worthy sages who transcend the world.
If the Sangha is such as this, can it not be revered?
Master Yuan of Gushan instructs his disciples: Alas! The Great Dharma has declined, and our distance from the Sages grows ever greater.
Though those who wear the black robes are numerous, those who truly seek the Way are exceedingly rare.
They compete for fame and profit as their own achievement,
regarding the propagation of the Dharma as a mere child's play.
Consequently, the gates of the Dharma have rarely been opened and the net of the teachings is on the verge of collapsing.
We truly rely upon future generations to sustain this Way.
You all must empty your minds to request the Dharma and purify yourselves to rely upon your teachers.
In the near term, you shall establish yourself and bring renown;
in the distant future, you shall hope to transform the mundane into the sacred.
To propagate the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpa-dharma*), whom else but you could I entrust this?
Therefore, you must cultivate yourself and practice what you preach, being as careful at the end as you were at the beginning.
Diligently pursue your studies and be prudent in your conduct and withdrawal from the world.
Shun evil companions as you would avoid tigers and wolves.
Serve good friends as you would your own parents;
serve the teacher with full ritual propriety and be willing to sacrifice your life for the sake of the Dharma.
When there is a virtuous mother, she naturally takes pride in her child.
If faults arise, rectify them with the utmost speed;
remain firm and unshakable in upholding benevolence and righteousness;
and when dwelling in poverty and low station, take such joy that one forgets all sorrow.
That which is natural diverges from calamity and converges with fortune;
how could it depend on comparing appearances or asking about destiny to seek the timing of honor and success?
To select auspicious days and times merely to escape the misfortunes of the *Pi* and *Zun* hexagrams—
how could this be the far-reaching insight of a śramaṇa?
It is truly but the deluded sentiment of a worldly person.
It is only fitting that upon seeing the worthy, one should think of emulating them;
when it comes to practicing benevolence, one should not yield.
Thus, he yearned for the Dharma-seekers of the Snowy Mountains.
Emulating Sudhana in his quest for teachers,
he found that fame and profit were insufficient to move his heart.
One need not worry about the anxieties of birth and death;
should one's merit be perfected and the task accomplished,
one will surely travel from the near to the far.
Without seeking fame, fame spreads of itself;
without summoning the multitude, the multitude arrives of its own accord;
his wisdom is sufficient to illuminate delusion.
Compassion is sufficient to gather people in.
In times of adversity, one perfects oneself;
in times of success, one benefits the whole world.
He caused the true wind to cease and then rise again;
when the torch of wisdom had been extinguished, he made it shine once more.
He may truly be called a great man.
He may truly be called an emissary of the Tathāgata.
How could he allow his person to dwell in lecture halls while his traces are mixed with those of ordinary disciples?
Amidst filth and corruption, they feel no hesitation;
in their conduct and understanding, they perceive nothing to be feared.
Thus, through the accumulation of habits until they become second nature, they bring about their own destruction.
At first they admire those superior sages,
yet in the end they sink into the lowest evils.
Such people as these are truly pitiable.
The Odes say, "There is nothing that does not have a beginning, yet few are able to reach the end.
This is precisely what it means.
Should those of superior capacity not take this as a warning?
Furthermore, although the categories of precepts and wisdom diverge into the distinct traditions of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, all emerge from the Buddha-mind;
their intent lies in the Dharma-realm, where they ultimately converge.
Since they had not yet understood the Great Way,
each party instead relied upon their own particular positions;
those who studied the sutras and śāstras consequently treated the training in the precepts as something to be discarded.
Those in the schools of Sectarian Vinaya rely on sutras and śāstras as mere empty talk;
those who practice the Great Dharma cause the Lesser Vehicle to perish,
while those who listen to the Lesser Vehicle disparage and revile the Great Dharma.
Seeing only that the Teacher of Men praised one side in particular,
they clung to it and engaged in mutual disputes over right and wrong;
how could they know that the Buddha’s intent is ever harmonious?
If one attains this realization without perceiving "self" and "other," they should mutually support and assist one another,
together bringing the conditions for awakening to maturity.
It is like the myriad streams flowing toward the capital; there are none that do not reach the sea.
When the hundred officials attend to their duties, they all say they are serving the King.
I have never seen anyone protect a single stream while intending to block the many currents.
To wish to abandon the myriad accomplishments while guarding only a single office—
considering the original intent behind the Dharma King’s dissemination of transformation,
he presided over all categories of beings, each with its own designated administration.
The Minor Vinaya compares with the relative weight of ritual and penal law;
the Mahāyāna resembles the responsibility of the balance scale.
Cultivating merit is like overseeing the transport of grain by water and land.
If the composition [of these works] were managed by the words of the sovereign,
then all the hundred officials of the state would cultivate them;
likewise, the various schools of our teaching would compete to expound them.
If one clearly understands this principle, how could one cling to heterodox views?
One must surely assess one's own talent and propagate [the teaching] according to one's capacity.
Those of keen nature may study various fields to cultivate goodness;
those of shallow understanding should confine themselves to a single school.
If this is so, then although each may disseminate their own style and influence, [they remain distinct].
Together they accomplish compassionate relief,
collectively returning to the ocean of harmony and union,
and sitting together upon the couch of liberation.
Thus, you are truly a guide for those lost on the path and a wooden clapper for the gates of the Teaching.
Occupying the position of a master, you are surely free from any sense of unworthiness.
You will proceed toward the fruit of Buddhahood with absolute certainty and without doubt.
Do not harbor pride or self-aggrandizement over your minor insights and knowledge,
nor establish a great sense of self-importance.
He treats those who have attained awakening with contempt and deludes those who follow him;
though it is said that he listens and seeks [the truth], he has not remedied his faults,
even if some of his words happen to be correct.
"You all must reflect upon this.

Exert yourselves in study! Exert yourselves in study! This preface to "Exhortation to Study" was composed because, while people of middling capacity know how to apply themselves to learning, some nevertheless fall away from it.
Thus, I have written this "Exhortation to Study."
Alas! Learning must not be neglected for even a moment;
the Way must not be departed from for even a moment.
Since the Way is clarified through learning, how could one neglect learning?
The realm of the sages and worthies is reached through the Way.
Can the Way be abandoned?
Thus, if the learning of ordinary people is not indolent, they can attain the state of a worthy.
If the learning of a worthy person is not indolent, they can reach the level of a sage.
Ran Qiu’s learning could have reached that of Yan Yuan;
that he fell short of embodying the full measure was due solely to indolence of heart.
Therefore it is said:
"It is not that I do not speak of the Way; rather, your power is insufficient.
The Master said:
Those who suffer from a lack of strength abandon their path midway;
now you have made a painting.
Yan Yuan’s learning could have reached the level of the Master.
Those who do not equal the Sage Teacher simply meet an early death; had they not died,
how could one have known they were not the equal of Zhongni?
It was because his learning was never flagging.
Thus it is said:
"There was the son of the Yan family who loved learning; unfortunately, he met an early death."
Nowadays, however, such people are non-existent.
Someone asked:
"Does a sage learn?"
He said, "What words are these?
What words are these?
Even ordinary people and the worthy know to learn."
Could it be that the Sage was indolent in his studies?
Indeed, Heaven is firm, yet it was able to learn suppleness from Earth; therefore—
It does not act in accordance with the four seasons;
for although the earth is yielding, it is able to learn firmness from Heaven. Therefore, it is so.
It is capable of producing metal and stone.
Although Yang brings about generation,
it also learns the severity of killing from Yin.
The soft grasses wither and die therein;
this is the stern and destructive nature of the Yin.
Yet, because it also learns to give rise to growth through the Yang, [it does not remain in its destructive state].
Chives and wheat grow there.
Now, are they heaven? Are they earth? Are they yang? Are they yin?
They study one another in mutual interaction without ever wearying.
Thus all things are brought to completion.
If Heaven did not learn suppleness, it would have nothing with which to cover;
if Earth did not learn firmness, it would have nothing with which to support.
If Yang does not learn from Yin, there is no means by which it can be opened;
if Yin does not learn from Yang, there is no means by which it can be closed.
The Sage has nothing else [but this].
"Thus, Heaven and Earth, Yin and Yang, and the four seasons proceed; these are the things one studies without indolence.
Where would a sage find indolence?
Thereupon, someone left his seat and said:
I am a solitary and ignorant person;
it is my good fortune that you have dispelled my delusions.
I wish to hear about the learning of the Sage.
The Master of the Zhongyong said:
"Sit down again, and I shall speak to you.
Does the Book not say?"
"Only the madman who can maintain mindfulness becomes a sage;
only the sage who lacks mindfulness becomes mad.
Therefore, even in moments of haste or distress, a sage never fails to mindfully contemplate and study the Right Path."
The Master was a Great Sage.
He rose far above his peers and stood out from his kind;
since the birth of mankind, there has never been anyone like the Master.
"When entering the Grand Ancestral Temple, he asks about every matter;
this means he is learning from those within the temple.
When three people walk together, he chooses the good among them and follows it."
Thus, he studied with Jiexing.
Upon entering the Zhou state, he inquired about the rites from Laozi;
thus, he studied with the Grand Scribe.
Is it that the sagehood of Zhongni was not equal to that of the temple attendants, the ritual officers, or the court chroniclers?
It is rather because the sage feared that if one studied without keeping the correct Way in mind,
one would end up becoming a madman.
Therefore it is said:
"One must certainly possess the loyalty and trustworthiness of Qiu;
one must simply not match Qiu’s love for learning."
It is said: "The sage is born knowing; why must he learn?
It is replied: "To know and yet learn is the way of the sage.
To learn and then know is the way of the ordinary person."
Neither sages nor ordinary people are without their reliance on learning.
Confucius said,
"The gentleman cannot but learn."
Zilu said, "In the Southern Mountains there is bamboo that is straight naturally without being bent.

he values only the ability to seize the opportune moment, respond with adaptability, resolve entanglements, and blunt the enemy's edge;
he observes only the sharpness of his intellectual blade and the acuity of his verbal thrusts.
They had completely forgotten its meaning and sought no liberation from suffering.
Master Yuanyang of Jiangbiao lamented that the Dharma of Chan had not yet spread there;
he therefore sought it with great diligence and finally obtained it.
The Patriarch Bodhidharma,
observing the karmic conditions of this land and confronting the chaos of this era, [proceeded as follows].
He then proclaimed:
"I do not establish written words," thereby seeking to dispel their attachment to texts and their stagnation in pursuing them.
"Directly pointing at the human mind" clarifies that one suddenly realizes the state of non-arising;
its mechanism is steep and its principle is perfect.
Consequently, those who advocate for gradual cultivation have persistently subjected this tradition to slander and defamation.
As for the transmission of the Dharma of Chan, it began with Bodhidharma;
directly descending from him, the robe was passed down through six successive generations.
Branching out in all directions, they are beyond counting, as clarified in the *Baolin Zhuan* (The Record of the Treasure Grove) of Caoxi.
Master Daofa’s annotated edition excised the original text under the heading "Directly Pointing at the Human Mind"; here, we restore it according to the original version.

Record of the Hall for Selecting Buddhas at Baofeng Chan Monastery in Hongzhou, composed by Chancellor Zhang Shangying. During the Chongning era, the Son of Heaven bestowed the title "Compassionate Response" (*Cisheng*) upon the stupa of Mazu.
His posthumous title was Zuyin.
One monk was ordained each year to serve as an offering for the incense and lamps.
The old man dwelling on the mountain possessed profound merit;
he immediately constructed the Celestial Scripture Pavilion behind the Patriarch’s Hall and established a hall supported by that pavilion.
He named it "Selecting the Buddha" and requested that his disciples ask me for a record of this.
I declined three times, but their request became increasingly insistent.
I said to him, "The ancients spoke of 'selecting a Buddha' and 'passing the examination' as being merely matters of names and words.
Yet you have used such terms to name your hall."
I have recorded this once more.
Is it not improper? Out of pity for your diligence, I have composed this record for you.
Now, "selection" (xuan) refers to the act of choosing.
There is rejecting and accepting, as well as excellence and inferiority.

Bestowing [the title] upon those who succeed in the civil service examinations and employing them among the talented—this was the means by which the ancient kings encouraged the age and sharpened the dull-witted.
It was not the means for selecting Buddhas; for if a Buddha were something that could be selected, [it would be no different].
Do you take it to be the six sense organs?
Do you take it to be the six sense objects?
Or do you take it to be the six consciousnesses?
If one were to accept the "three sixes," then all ordinary beings could become Buddhas;
yet if one rejects the "three sixes," who would cultivate or realize the immeasurable Buddha-dharmas?
[Therefore, one should] accept the Four Truths, the Six Perfections, the Seven Factors of Enlightenment, the Eightfold Path, the Nine Meditative Concentrations, and the Ten Fearlessnesses.
Up to and including the eighteen unique qualities and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—
if one grasps them, there are dharmas.
It transcends the Four Noble Truths, the Six Perfections,
and even the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. How could it be categorized as a mere chapter?
To eliminate them is to lack the Dharma.
To eliminate or grasp at existence and non-existence is as subtle as a single strand of silk lingering in the mind.
Suddenly, it is as if fine dust has entered the breast.
This is found in the Sūtra Piṭaka,
where it is sometimes referred to as the two obstacles (āvaraṇa).
Some call it the four illnesses;
some call it the provisional meaning (neyārtha);
others call it conceptual proliferation (prapañca).
Some call it the false view of pervasive conceptualization;
others call it the subtle outflow.
To grasp it is not the Buddha.
To reject it is not to be a Buddha;
yet to neither reject nor grasp it is likewise not to be a Buddha.
Can the fruit of Buddhahood be attained through selection?
He said, "The Master's discourse on the School of Characteristics is like my ancestors' discourse on the School of Chan.
For all those whom I have selected, it is simply a matter of the mind being empty."
The disciple constructs the hall and poses a question;
the master sits cross-legged and provides an answer,
sometimes revealing the profound and the essential.
Sometimes he showed them through discernment;
sometimes he showed them through the Dharma-mirror Samādhi;
and sometimes he showed them through the causes and conditions of the Eye of the Path.
Sometimes he points to the path that goes beyond;
sometimes he points to the final phrase;
sometimes he points directly at the head.
Sometimes he showed them the plain and real;
sometimes he raised his eyebrows and blinked his eyes;
sometimes he brandished his whisk or struck the meditation seat.
One may draw a circular mark,
or make a single stroke,
or clap one's hands.
Or, those who perform dances that accord with my spiritual capacity know that the mind is empty;
knowing that the mind is empty, [they act accordingly].
"Then the fruit of Buddhahood can be selected. I said:
"When the World-Honored One raised the flower, Kāśyapa smiled."
The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is simply this.
Yet, how numerous and diverse are the instructions of the masters of later generations!
I fear that the teaching of Śākyamuni will decline from this point on.
Shen was a native of Hedong;
he was content with coarse food and endured hardships.
Having long traveled with Zhenjing of Guansi, he stands solitary and firm;
he will surely be able to propagate the Teaching.
Indeed, the teaching of the Śākya clan leaves the body behind through the cultivation of emaciation.
In solitude, he stilled his thoughts;
through the secret practice of precepts and meditative concentration, even ghosts and spirits could not fathom him.
The wondrous application of his compassion was shared by both the hidden and the manifest worlds.
If one responds only after being pressed from above,
then our assembly will lose its companions;
if one speaks only when driven by necessity, then the six groups will lose their boundaries.
The transformation from life to death is what people fear.
I have never been born; how then could there be death?
Thus, what is there to fear?
The realm of profit and harm is that which people choose between;
I have never possessed profit, so how could there be harm?
Thus, what need is there for choice?
In this way, it is not that the external is non-empty while the internal is empty of itself;
it is not that the objective realm is non-empty while the mind is empty of itself;
it is not that phenomena are non-empty while principle is empty of itself.
It is not empty of its characteristics, yet its nature is inherently empty;
it is not empty of emptiness, yet emptiness itself is empty.
Emptiness is equality, and equality is the Great.
Greatness is round; being round, it is wondrous.
Being wondrous, it is the Buddha.
Alas! It is with this that I look toward you.
My son, do not neglect this!

The Inscription on Faith in Mind by Chan Master Jianzhi, the Third Patriarch. The Inscription on Faith in Mind by Chan Master Jianzhi, the Third Patriarch: "The Ultimate Way is without difficulty; it is only that one dislikes discrimination."
Simply do not harbor likes or dislikes, and you will be luminously clear and bright.
A difference of even a hair’s breadth results in worlds as far apart as heaven and earth.
If you wish to attain realization before you, do not maintain any notions of favorability or opposition.
The conflict between the opposing states of compliance and resistance is a sickness of the mind;
failing to recognize the profound essence, one’s efforts to contemplate stillness are in vain.
Perfectly identical to the great void, it is neither deficient nor superfluous.
It is precisely because of grasping and rejecting that one falls short.
Do not pursue what has conditions; do not dwell in the patience of emptiness.
With a single state of equanimity, all things subside of themselves.
When stillness returns to stillness, stillness moves even more; when movement returns to stillness, stillness moves even further.
If one merely stagnates in these two extremes, how can one know the single principle?
If the single principle is not penetrated, both sides fail in their function.
To dispatch existence and non-existence is to turn one's back on emptiness;
excessive speech and excessive thought increasingly become inconsistent with the truth.
When speech is cut off and thought is extinguished, there is nowhere that does not penetrate.
To return to the root is to attain the essential meaning; to follow after illumination is to lose the fundamental principle.
A moment of returning-illumination surpasses the previous emptiness.
That the previous emptiness underwent transformation was entirely due to deluded vision.
Do not seek to attain truth; simply require the cessation of views.
When the two views do not abide, be careful not to pursue them.
As soon as there is right and wrong, one becomes distracted and loses the mind.
Second, because existence arises from unity, one should not cling even to that.
When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault.
Being without fault, there are no dharmas; thus, neither the mind nor its phenomena arise.
The capacity can subside according to the object, and the object sinks as it pursues the capacity;
the object arises through the capacity and the capacity arises through the object.
If one wishes to know these two segments, they are fundamentally one emptiness.
The single emptiness is identical to the two polarities, encompassing all phenomena equally.
When neither the refined nor the coarse is perceived, how could there be partiality?
The substance of the Great Way is vast; it is neither easy nor difficult.
With narrow views and lingering doubts, one becomes increasingly frantic and increasingly sluggish;
by clinging to them, one loses the proper measure and inevitably enters a deviant path.
By letting go naturally, the essence has neither departure nor abiding.
To act spontaneously in accord with the Way is to roam in leisure, free from affliction;
to bind one's thoughts contrary to the Truth leads to dullness and is not good.
If it is not good to labor the spirit, what use is there for distinguishing between the distant and the intimate?
If you wish to attain the One Vehicle, do not revile the six sense objects.
When the six sense objects are not reviled, one returns to the same state as perfect enlightenment.
The wise are non-active; the foolish bind themselves.
In the Dharma there is no separate dharma, yet one falsely clings to it with self-attachment.
To employ the mind by means of the mind—is this not a great error?
Delusion gives rise to stillness and agitation; awakening is free from likes and dislikes.
All dualistic extremes arise solely from mental deliberation;
why labor to grasp at dreams, illusions, and empty flowers?
Let gain and loss, right and wrong, be relinquished all at once.
If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams naturally vanish;
if the mind does not diverge, the myriad dharmas are as one.
This single suchness is profound in its essence; standing aloof, one forgets all conditions.
When the myriad dharmas are viewed together, they return to and merge with spontaneity.
That which causes them to vanish cannot be compared to anything else.
In stillness there is no movement; in movement there is no stillness.
Since duality is not established, how can there be unity?
Ultimately and exhaustively, no fixed rules exist;
the mind accords with equality, and all that is done comes to rest.
Doubts are completely purified, and right faith becomes harmonious and upright.
Nothing remains to be clung to, and there is nothing to be remembered.
Empty clarity illuminates itself spontaneously, without taxing the mind or strength.
Beyond the sphere of discursive thought, it is difficult for consciousness and emotion to fathom.
In the *tathatā* dharma-realm, there is neither other nor self;
one must urgently achieve resonance, realizing that only non-duality exists.
Non-dual and identical, it encompasses all without exception;
the wise of the ten directions all enter this school.
This school is neither constricted nor extended—a single thought-moment is ten thousand years.
Neither abiding nor non-abiding, it is present before the eyes throughout the ten directions.
The smallest is identical to the great, forgetting and severing all boundaries;
the greatest is identical to the small, with no visible limits or surface.
Existence is non-existence, and non-existence is existence.
If it were not thus, one would certainly not need to maintain [this practice]. One is all, and all is one.
If one can simply act in this way, what need is there to worry about anything not being accomplished?
The mind of faith is non-dual; non-dual is the mind of faith.
It transcends the path of words and is neither past, future, nor present.
Regarding the three trainings of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, the *Zizhi* states:
"All Buddha-dharmas do not transcend these three trainings.
Because sentient beings delude their minds, they give rise to afflictions; because their thoughts are stirred, they form karma."
Because birth and death are endless due to the retribution of karma,
one who wishes to escape the fruit of suffering must eliminate its cause.
Therefore, one first uses the precepts to rectify that karma.
Next, one clarifies their delusions through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Because karma is divided into good and evil, the two practices of cessation (*śamatha*) and application (*pragraha*) serve as mutual antidotes; likewise, because delusion consists solely of torpor and agitation, they are likewise countered.
The two dharmas of concentration and wisdom are applied as antidotes.
When the illness is cured by the medicine, the faculties rely upon the teachings for cultivation;
thereafter, karma is exhausted and delusions are eliminated.
When emotion ceases, the fundamental nature is revealed.
Though the gates of the teachings are vast, they do not transcend this.

Regarding the four reliances for interpreting the Dharma: when one relies on the four reliances for interpreting the Dharma, one sees that the Patriarch’s profound intention ultimately points toward the definitive meaning—relying on the Dharma and not relying on the person.
In humans, there is only the existence of mental states;
in phenomena, there is the pattern of the norm.
The emptiness of nature is the true nature; this emptiness of nature pervades both the Mahayana and Hinayana. Its essence is free from delusion.
One should take this very method as the reliance for the True Dharma.

The Nirvāṇa Sūtra clearly elucidates this path in its ultimate teaching: "To rely on the Dharma" means to rely on the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena); "not to rely on persons" means not to rely on Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. If one can turn back from that worldly mind...
Relying upon the authoritative measure of the Sage,
one conceals the mind while engaging in activities, knowing that they are not inherently existent; by maintaining this mind as the path,
one portion of knowledge realizes non-existence and clearly accords with the principle of emptiness.
The first part, contemplating revulsion and clarifying the violation of objective phenomena,
is called the method of settling the mind through the practice of entering the true path of *dharmatā*.
"Relying on the meaning, not on the words" refers to this.
"Speech" refers to verbal expression;
"stopping" has the meaning of laying aside the fishing trap.

This is because once one attains the principle and understands the way of transforming things—where "transformation" implies change—one cuts off deliberation and blocks speech after having realized and understood.
"Even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharmas.
Thus, the sutras contain the metaphor of abandoning the raft.

People cherish the discourse on "witnessing with the eyes"; as Zhuangzi said, "The Way exists through witnessing with the eyes"—is this not because when the meaning is grasped, the verbal expression ceases?

Regarding the statement that the "excellent finger" is like the moon, it is not appropriate for one not to understand this. What was clarified above was the meaning of the provisional; now, by means of language, the meaning of the ultimate manifestation is revealed, and language itself is set aside. Now I say: having attained the meaning, the meaning is itself the word.
One who truly practices the Way constantly contemplates and constantly deconstructs the conventional.
One contemplates that words are conventional and thus refutes their adherence to literal meaning.

That is to say, when speech follows meaning, it is still merely the recitation of words; when one attains the meaning and forgets the words, one must still eliminate the notion that the meaning has any inherent existence. As for "rely on wisdom, do not rely on consciousness":
Consciousness refers to the manifestation of perceptions that follow after sensory objects;
when the eyes and ears are infatuated with forms and sounds,
one fails to awaken and becomes equal to oxen and sheep.

Delivering those who are like ordinary beings and heretics, they practice together to clarify the six consciousnesses; since deluded thoughts are shared by both humans and animals, there is the consequence of falling into the lower realms. Now, instructing them to rely upon Buddha-wisdom—that is, the contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)—the faults are gradually diminished and clarity increases. The Great Sage has shown that the teaching regarding objects is that they are one's own mind.
Those of the lowest ignorance stubbornly cling to the notion that sensory objects exist outside of consciousness;
thus, there is no way to guide them toward transformation or cause them to relinquish such views.

It is known, therefore, that those who remain stuck in ordinary consciousness and whose deluded minds are overturned by inversion constantly wander through the three inversions throughout their transmigrations.
Courageously exerting oneself with exceptional penetration, one knows thoughts as they arise;
knowing that which is inverted and difficult to purify is called "reliant consciousness" (āśrita-vijñāna),
while knowing the flow that must be reversed is called "wisdom according to its scope" (yathābhūmi-jñāna).
By thus applying effort, clarity and magnitude gradually increase.
Later, upon seeing objects of the sensory realm, one knows they do not come from outside;
that the objects are not external to the mind, but are manifestations of one's own mind.
How could there be such deluded beings who give rise to hatred and attachment,
yet fail to investigate thoroughly until they understand that [the self] is distinct from cattle and sheep?
Regarding the reliance on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) rather than those of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*):
both of these types of sūtras are the authoritative word of the Sage (*āptavāda*).
Those who first enter the Path must understand this distinction.
Thus, there is nothing obstructed or unpenetrated, and all doubts are resolved.

However, because the natures, cognitions, depths, and capacities of sentient beings differ, the Great Sage has provided distinct teachings according to their dispositions. Nevertheless, based on the ultimate Way, it is simply one’s own mind.
The Sūtra says:
"The phenomena of the three realms, whether superior or inferior, I declare to be nothing but mind.
This clarifies the mind in terms of the world as the environment-retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).
It is further stated:

"The Tathāgata has taught that suchness, the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), nirvāṇa, the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and the various types of mind-made bodies are all merely the measure of mind (cittamātra).
This is based on the supramundane essence of phenomena to clarify the nature of the mind.
Ultimately reaching the ultimate reality, one arrives at this very source.
Following the stream to respond to conditions, one returns to the fundamental, definitive meaning.

Regarding the precepts, they are exclusively those established by the Buddha and do not apply to others; regarding conduct, they are exclusively those established by the Buddha and do not apply to others. Thus says the *Xingzong lun* (Treatise on the Source of Conduct).
Within the great trichiliocosm, the Buddha is the Dharma King;
the Vinaya is his decree,
established solely by the Sage.
All other lower ranks may merely rely upon and follow them;
this is truly because the Tathāgata’s practice and fruition are perfectly complete,
having fully exhausted the nature of the light and heavy karmas of all sentient beings.
Even those below the level of Perfect Enlightenment (Samyaksambuddha) are not yet capable of it,
let alone other minor sages who would dare to venture upon such deliberation.
It is like the state’s rewards, punishments, and edicts,
which must necessarily issue from the king;
if ministers usurp authority or commoners violate their word, disorder ensues.
There will be no day when ruin does not come;
the Buddha-dharma is likewise.
If it permits others to speak against it, sentient beings will not uphold it.
This is because the Dharma will not long endure.
To summarize various texts in order to praise the precepts, the *Zizhi* (Commentary on the Support) quotes the "Statement of the Fundamental Tenet," which says:
This is because you are the Great Teacher who is able to provide a standard for all things.
Or it is said:
"The feet of a person are capable of reaching wherever they must go."
Some say: "The great earth is that which generates, sustains, and maintains;
the pillars of the hall of the path-factors (mārgāṅga) are that upon which the holy path relies."
The citadel of meditative concentration (dhyāna) is that upon which both concentration and wisdom rely;
it is like a pond, like a mirror,
like a necklace, like a head, and like a vessel.
Furthermore, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is compared to heavy treasure,
to life, to a boat, and to the wings of a bird;
these may be understood by looking into that work.
Furthermore, within the *Piñjū* (sections on the categories of offenses), the protection of the precepts is first elucidated by enumerating eight similes,
such as "like the youngest son of a king" and "like the light of the moon."
It is like a wish-fulfilling gem; like an only son to a king;
like the single eye of a person; like provisions for the poor;
like a beloved kingdom to a king; and like an excellent medicine for the sick.
Furthermore, the Great Preface to the Precepts is like the boundless ocean and like jewels that one never tires of;
the *Sāṃghāṭī-śīla-mūla* is like a chain for a monkey or a bridle for a horse.
These matters are detailed in the Sūtras and Vinayas, so I shall not cite them further at length.
This is truly because the virtue of the precepts is so lofty and vast that it cannot be illustrated by any single object; rather,
various images have been cited individually, each capturing but one aspect.
It cannot be entirely similar.
It is said that when the Buddha was in the world, he especially propagated the Dharma of the precepts;
furthermore, although he discussed various scriptures...
Nevertheless, one must pay the greatest attention to the Vinaya;
thus, the *Piñjū* (Skandhaka) states:
"The World-Honored One, dwelling in the world, profoundly understood the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings."
In all actions one undertakes, one must take dignified decorum as the primary guide;
this is correct.
Furthermore, the sutras are spoken by others as well.
The Vinaya was proclaimed solely from the Buddha’s own golden mouth;
even those of great authority, acting as his shadow and echo, knew only to revere it.
How much less would other lesser sages dare to offer their own words?
Furthermore, while various sūtras speak of temporal limitations,
the Vinaya encompasses the meaning from beginning to end.
The *Shuochao* states:
Beginning at the Deer Park and ending at the Śāla Grove,
he established precepts according to the capacities of beings,
resulting in ten thousand variations.
Possessing these three intentions, it is forever distinct from other sutras;
thus, the claim that its extensive exposition is flavorless is surely a misconception.
Regarding the demonstration of the broad and concise characteristics of the precepts for monks and nuns, the *Sengni jieshang guanglüe shichao* states:
Question: In the Vinaya, it is stated that the Saṃgha enumerates two hundred and fifty precepts, while the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* contains them in full for monks;

for nuns, however, there are five hundred. Is this statement true or false? This mention of "five hundred" appears in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, yet it differs from the Vinaya; therefore, I ask for a resolution. Answer: Both lists provide fixed numbers as a general indication. "General" (*yue*) means "abbreviated" (*lüe*). Thus, the various schools generally state that one need not rely strictly upon these specific numbers.
Discoursing on its essential nature, the precept-substance is solely non-action;
yet when its characteristics are clarified in relation to objects,
they are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Furthermore, one merely points to the two hundred and fifty rules as the path for observing and violating precepts.
Within the Vinaya, there are three hundred and forty-eight rules for bhikṣuṇīs;
these may be pointed to as that which is to be guarded against.
Now, according to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*,
the dharma for receiving the precepts by bhikṣuṇīs is brief, numbering five hundred,
and extensive, numbering eighty thousand.
The monastic rules for monks consist briefly of two hundred and fifty precepts;
in detail, they are the same as those in the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*.
Regarding the intent behind the teaching on ordaining nuns, the *Duyi jiaoyi ye shu* (Commentary on the Intent and Karma of Ordaining Nuns) states:

Regarding the occasion for women to enter the monastic order, the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with five hundred women, deeply loathed birth and death upon hearing that the Buddha had renounced the world;
they sought ordination from the Buddha.
Because he would not have been able to propagate the Way extensively or bring benefit through far-reaching transformation,
[the Buddha] suppressed him and did not grant permission.
Later, when he returned to Śrāvastī, he shaved his hair and donned the robes himself.
Standing by the monastery, he prayed to be permitted to receive the precepts.
He made this request three times, whereupon the precepts were conferred. He must then respectfully uphold the Dharma and ensure that he practices it in full accordance with the rules.
Thereupon, he was immediately ordained with the full precepts.
The record states:
"Women are base and weak; few people have respect and faith."
Therefore, there is no benefit from extensive propagation;
on the contrary, it further brings disgrace upon the True Dharma and causes it to diminish by half,
because the Buddha did not permit it.
Returning once more to the city, he immediately transformed his appearance and went again to the Jetavana Monastery, where he stood leaning against the gate.
Ānanda interceded on his behalf and petitioned the Buddha.
He was commanded to transmit the teachings.
Being able to practice the eight respects, he was immediately granted ordination; upon hearing this, Mahāprajāpatī and the others likewise developed the aspiration for full ordination.
The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) further states:
"Regarding those who receive [the precepts] before an assembly of twenty,
this is intended to clarify that because women’s karmic retribution involves deep delusions and shallow wisdom, they are prone to giving rise to arrogance and indolence."
If one must receive full ordination, there must be ten monks and ten nuns respectively;
only then will the superior mind arise.
It is also said:

If one examines the monastic histories prior to the Song dynasty in China, it is recorded that the entire community of nuns received their vows from the community of bhikṣus, as is the case with those who receive the Eight Respectful Precepts according to the various Vinayas.
However, because the remaining five hundred nuns and the eleven assemblies accepted it, they exclusively cherished the Path.
Guṇavarman— translated here as "Virtuous Armor"— is what the Noble One (Ārya) says.
If there are not two assemblies but only one assembly receiving [the ordination],
it is permissible as in the case of Mahāprajāpatī. How is this known?
Furthermore, when discussing the fundamental dharma, it stops at the preliminary preparations;
since nothing yet has been accomplished,
we must revert to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) within the Saṃgha.
Subsequently, eleven nuns from Sīhaladvīpa (Lion Island), including Tiexuoluo (Tiśrā), felt inspired to study the Song language;
they were received by both the assembly of monks and the assembly of nuns.

Regarding the Eight Respectful Precepts for Nuns (*bhikṣuṇī-aṣṭa-guru-dharma*), the *Nisengbiao* (Section on the Nun’s Assembly) of the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao* states: [The text continues with the citation of the precepts.]
The Buddha Bhadraśikhi did not initially allow women to leave the household life and become ordained,
for fear that it would cause the True Dharma to perish five hundred years earlier. However, five hundred years later, he taught the Eight Rules of Respect and permitted their ordination.
By practicing according to the teachings,
one regains a lifespan of a thousand years;
because they are not practiced now, the Dharma perishes everywhere.
The Huizheng ji states:
Fourteen years after the Buddha attained enlightenment,
his maternal aunt requested to leave the household life.
The Buddha did not permit her ordination.
Ānanda made his request three times,
and the Buddha instructed Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra to convey the Eight Rules of Respect to her.
"If you are able to practice it, I shall permit you to go forth.
He replied, "I shall receive and uphold it with the highest reverence."
Regarding the "Eight Respects": first,
when a bhikṣuṇī who has been ordained for a hundred years sees a bhikṣu who has newly received the precepts,
she must rise to meet him, escort him, prostrate, inquire after his well-being, and request that he be seated.
Second, a bhikṣuṇī must not revile or slander a bhikṣu.
Third, she must not expose a bhikṣu’s offenses or speak of his faults;
whereas a bhikṣu may speak of a bhikṣuṇī’s faults.
Fourth, a śikṣamāṇā who has already trained in the precepts should seek to receive the full ordination from the Saṃgha.
Fifth, a bhikṣuṇī who has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Sixth, she should perform the *mānatva* penance before both assemblies of monks every half-month.
Seventh, within each half-month, she must seek out a teacher for instruction from among the community of monks.
Eighth, she should not observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*) in a place where there are no monks.
Eighth, when the summer retreat has concluded, one should go before the Saṃgha and request a person to perform the *pravāraṇā*.
These eight rules should be honored, revered, and praised;

If one harbors deep faith,
how could one hesitate to practice accordingly? Thus, Master Jingxi’s *Fuxing Ji* states:
Some say: "Regarding all things that one does not perceive as belonging to oneself, if they are beneficial,
why should one perform the ritual of 'purifying' (śuddhi) before using them?"
Now, these things you ask about are not already your own wealth;
why would they not suffice for the four seas?
Use whatever is beneficial.
Why not simply entrust [the goods] to the two fields—the field of compassion and the field of reverence—and place them in a secure room, sealed within a chest or casket?

To harbor thoughts of personal ownership would surely lead to the transgression of theft; yet to treat them as one's own property would likewise violate the rules for the purification of offerings (śuddhi-vyavahāra).
What contradiction is there in principle to giving after having performed the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*)?
Let it be as one’s own mind intends, for others will subsequently follow one’s example.
Therefore, one should know that not reciting the *śuddhika* (purity formula) is profoundly contrary to the Buddha’s intention and is not subsumed within either of the two vehicles.
The three faculties are not restrained.
If this is what it means to leave the household life, is it not a case of wasting one's potential in vain?
Regarding the "Eight Impure Wealths that Increase Greed and Ruin the Path," the *Chao* (Excerpts) states: [text follows].

because those in such matters have limited capacities and narrow intentions,

"If among the disciples there is no one to provide for their needs, and the world suffers from famine such that food and drink are difficult to obtain..."
In order to protect, maintain, and establish the True Dharma,

I have permitted my disciples to accept, possess, and trade in gold, silver, vehicles, fields, houses, grain, and other necessities. Although I have permitted their acceptance and possession, [they must do so for the sake of the Dharma].
Items such as these must be given through a formal act of pure giving (*śuddha-dāna*).

The former clarifies that in the Mahāyāna, both the capacity of the practitioner (*mārga*) and the teaching (*śāsana*) are urgent; the latter clarifies that in the Hīnayāna, both the capacity and the teaching are gradual.

How much error has there been in the universal application of the Great Teaching!

I urge you to broaden your mind and benefit others according to the Way. From the *Sengwang pian* (Chapter on the Net of the Sangha): "I urge you to broaden your mind and benefit others according to the Way."
A sincere renunciant fears the manifold sufferings of the four enemies and loathes the impermanence of the three realms.
To bid farewell to the deepest affection of one's six kin and to renounce the profound attachment to the five desires is truly because the illusory and mundane world is worthy of being abandoned.
One should return to the path of truth;
it is fitting to broaden one's distant aspirations and purge base attachments,
not begrudging body or wealth as one upholds the True Dharma.
Moreover, since the Sangha’s food is taken from the ten directions for all to share equally,
it is only right that one should personally rejoice in it;
yet, human sentiments are narrow and biased, leading to unequal mental dispositions.
Is it not also laughable for some to close their doors and obstruct visiting monks?
Was that not the original intent of tolling the bell?
Having left the household life and abandoned attachments, one especially ought not to act in such a manner.
Yet, with this precarious and fragile body,
one cannot steadfastly protect the True Dharma;
with this fleeting and borrowed life, one is unwilling to reach far and wide.
For the Sangha to eat in such a manner violates the teachings of all Buddhas,
diminishes the merit of the donors,
and offends the sentiments of the assembly present.
This blocks the path for the Sangha of the ten directions;
as for the errors committed toward later generations, the resulting ruin will be far-reaching.

Would it not be excellent to reform former delusions and return to the Way? To be stingy with food and eat alone is the karma of a hungry ghost; this is called "great delusion. Someone may ask: "Matters concerning the Sangha are limited, while outside guests are infinite."
To provide limited food for an infinite number of monks—
this matter will certainly not succeed. He replied:
This is merely the shallow perspective of the vulgar and the narrow-mindedness of petty people.
How could it be considered the profound insight of pure wisdom or the lofty vision of a man of realization?
As for the offerings of the fourfold assembly:
The Triple Gem is a field of merit,
like the growth of heaven and earth or the resources provided by mountains and seas;
how could it ever be exhausted?
Therefore, the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* says:
"One should practice the Way with a single mind in accordance with the Dharma;
do not think of the necessities of food and clothing."
Even if one were to offer a single portion from within the Tathāgata’s mark of the white tuft of hair to all his ordained disciples,
it could not be exhausted.
Speaking from this perspective,
one should diligently cultivate the practice of the precepts and protect the Dharma with utmost sincerity;
gaining benefit through the Way and applying the Way universally.
It continues, saying:
"Even in secular teachings, it is said that one should worry about the Way rather than poverty;
how much more so for those who have left the household life, who transcend the mundane world?"
To not worry about protecting the Dharma but to worry about food and drink is a most grievous error.
Regarding the debate over whether the finger burned by the bodhisattva was large or small, the *Zizhi* (Fundamental Support) states: [text follows].
